Family Law Practice Guide

Child Custody and Parental Guardianship under Nepalese Family Law

📅 Published: 2025-03-25
🔄 Updated: 2025-10-01
⏱ 8 min read
🔍 Review: Senior Advocate Lead Counsel, Supreme Court Bar Association
Direct Legal Answer & Overview

Child custody in Nepal is governed by the paramount doctrine of the 'Best Interests of the Child' under Section 115 of the Muluki Civil Code 2074 and the Children Act 2075. By statutory rule: 1) A child under 5 years of age generally remains with the mother unless contrary to welfare; 2) A child between 5 and 14 years is placed based on mutual parental agreement or judicial evaluation of living conditions, schooling, and emotional stability; and 3) A child aged 14 or above may have their personal preference considered by the court. The non-custodial parent retains mandatory visitation rights and financial maintenance duties.

Key Practical Takeaways

  • Custody is not a proprietary right of either parent; the child welfare is the supreme legal standard.
  • Children under five years typically stay with the mother unless statutory exceptions apply.
  • Non-custodial parents possess statutory visitation rights and maintenance duties.

During marital separation, child custody is frequently the most emotionally charged issue. Nepalese law has evolved decisively from historic patriarchal traditions toward child-centric jurisprudence: the child is not the property of either parent, and their physical, educational, and emotional welfare overrides parental claims.

1. Statutory Age-Tier Guidelines under Section 115

Section 115 of the Muluki Civil Code 2074 establishes clear age-based guidelines:

  • Under 5 Years Old: The mother holds the primary statutory presumption of custody, provided she is capable of caring for the child, unless she voluntarily agrees otherwise.
  • Between 5 and 14 Years Old: Custody is determined by mutual parental agreement. If parents disagree, the court awards custody based on which parent offers superior emotional stability, educational continuity, and home environment.
  • 14 Years and Older: The court gives significant weight to the expressed wishes and preferences of the child.

2. Mandatory Visitation and Continuing Parental Responsibility

Depriving a parent of custody does not sever their parental bond. Under Section 117, the non-custodial parent holds an enforceable statutory right to regular visitation, weekend access, and holiday sharing. Furthermore, both parents remain legally bound to contribute proportionally to the child's living, healthcare, and educational expenses.

Statutory Citations & Governing Nepal Legislation

Statute / Act Section / Rule Legal Significance
Muluki Civil Code 2074 Section 114 to 121 (Care and Custody of Children) Statutory rules determining custody, maintenance, and parental responsibilities.
Children Act 2075 Section 7 (Best Interests of Child) Supreme legal principle governing all judicial decisions involving minors.

Documentary Checklist for this Procedure

  • ✔ Birth Registration Certificate of the minor child
  • ✔ Proof of schooling, medical care, and residential stability
  • ✔ Income and tax records of parents demonstrating capability to support child

Frequently Asked Questions on this Topic

Can a mother lose custody if she remarries in Nepal?

Under Section 115(2), remarrying does not automatically forfeit custody if the mother continues to provide a safe, nurturing environment. However, if the child welfare is compromised, the father or guardian can petition the court for a custody review.
